description: For **46** years South Africa organized racial segregation by law. **Nelson Mandela**, after **27** years in prison, helped the country leave it behind without a civil war.

hero.hook: A system of total segregation, and then a way out without civil war.

blocks.text: In **1948**, just as the world was starting to condemn state racism, South Africa took the opposite road. For **46 years** it organized total segregation by law: **[[apartheid]]**.

That regime collapsed in the early **1990s** without sliding into civil war. At the center of the turn stood **Nelson Mandela**, a lawyer turned resistance leader, freed after **27 years** behind bars.

The National Party put **[[apartheid]]** (“separateness” in Afrikaans) in place after May **1948**. Every citizen was classified: White, Black, Colored, Indian. That label decided the vote, the job, the place to live.

blocks.caption: Segregation signs: public space carved up by law

blocks.text: The **[[bantustans]]**, reserves meant to be “national homelands” for Black South Africans, covered only **13%** of the territory. Their real purpose was to strip those people of their South African citizenship. Without a pass there was no travel through white areas: prison was waiting.
For business reasons, Japanese visitors were officially classified as “honorary Whites.” Racism knew how to bend for a market.

The **[[ANC]]**, the African National Congress, organized the resistance. Mandela, born in **1918**, believed in non-violence at first. Then came the **[[Sharpeville massacre]]** (March **1960**): the police fired on an unarmed crowd protesting against the passes. **69** people were killed.

blocks.caption: Sharpeville, 1960: the turn toward armed struggle

blocks.text: The ANC was banned. Mandela co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe (“Spear of the Nation”) to sabotage the machinery of the regime. Arrested in **1962** and sentenced to life at the Rivonia Trial (**1964**), he became, on Robben Island, the most famous political prisoner in the world.

In the **1980s**, sanctions, an embargo and constant uprisings were suffocating the regime. **Frederik Willem de Klerk**, the white president who came to power in **1989**, understood that survival meant ending apartheid.

On **February 11, 1990**, Mandela walked out of prison. Four years of negotiation followed. In April **1994** came the first elections open to everyone: the ANC won and Mandela became president with **62.6%** of the vote, at the head of a government of national unity.

In **1995**, during the World Cup, Mandela pulled on the green jersey of the Springboks, the national rugby team long seen as an Afrikaner symbol. It was a gesture of reconciliation watched around the world.

With Archbishop **Desmond Tutu**, Mandela bet on reconciliation. The **[[Truth and Reconciliation Commission]]** offered amnesty in exchange for a full public confession: a form of **[[transitional justice]]** meant to uncover what had happened to the victims without tearing the country apart.
Mandela left power in **1999** after a single term. Legal racism was dead. Economic inequality, though, remains South Africa's great challenge.

events.detail: A massacre, and the turn to armed struggle.
events.title: Sharpeville

blocks.text: South African **[[apartheid]]** (**1948-1994**) was a system of racial segregation run by the state. Its fall, negotiated by Mandela and de Klerk, opened a multiracial democracy built on reconciliation.

title: Apartheid and Mandela
